skills.name: Use interval notation and solve linear inequalities in one unknown

note.text:
Interval notation writes a set of numbers by its ends.
• Square bracket: the end is included (≤ or ≥). Round bracket: the end is left out (< or >).
• −2 ≤ x < 5 is [−2, 5). x > 3 is (3, +∞). x ≤ 1 is (−∞, 1]. The symbol ∞ always has a round bracket.
On a number line, a filled circle means included and an open circle means left out.
Solve a linear inequality like an equation, with one extra rule: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number turns the sign round.
Example: −3x + 4 ≥ 10 → −3x ≥ 6 → x ≤ −2, that is (−∞, −2].

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to write sets of numbers in interval notation and solve linear inequalities, turning the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number.
Builds on: Form Three inequalities and the number line.
Leads to: absolute values (Lessons {17} and {18}), quadratic inequalities (Lesson {19}) and regions on graphs.

sections.heading: Interval notation
sections.text:
A set of numbers between two ends can be written with brackets.
• [a, b]: a ≤ x ≤ b, both ends included.
• (a, b): a < x < b, both ends left out.
• [a, b): a ≤ x < b.
• (a, +∞): x > a. (−∞, b]: x ≤ b. The symbol ∞ is never reached, so it always takes a round bracket.
Example: the ages of pupils in a class, at least {13} and under {16}, form {interval(13, 16, true, false)}.
On a number line: a filled circle for an included end, an open circle for one left out.

sections.heading: Solving and the negative rule
sections.text:
Treat an inequality like an equation: add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same number.
• {poly([3, 'x'], [-5, ''])} < x + {7} → {mono(2, 'x')} < {12} → x < {6}.
One extra rule: multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the sign round. Check with numbers: {2} < {5}, but {-2} > {-5}.
• {poly([-3, 'x'], [4, ''])} ≥ {10} → {mono(-3, 'x')} ≥ {6} → x ≤ {-2}, that is {interval('-inf', -2, false, true)}.

key_words.meaning: all the numbers between two ends, such as {interval(-1, 4, true, false)}
without end; it is never included

mistake.why: Dividing by {-2} turns the sign round. Check: x = {0} makes {mono(-2, 'x')} = {0} < {8}, and {0} > {-4}.

worked_example.problem: Solve {poly([a, 'x'], [b, ''])} < {poly([c, 'x'], [d, ''])} and write the answer in interval notation.
steps: Add {-b} to both sides: {mono(a - c, 'x')} < {d - b}.
Divide by {a - c}, a positive number, so the sign stays: x < {(d - b) / (a - c)}.
worked_example.answer: x < {(d - b) / (a - c)}, that is {interval('-inf', (d - b) / (a - c), false, false)}

cards.idea: Square brackets include the end; round brackets leave it out. ∞ always takes a round bracket.
Solve an inequality like an equation: do the same to both sides.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number turns the inequality sign round.

misconceptions.explain: Dividing by the negative number {-a} turns ≥ into ≤.
The sign ≥ includes the end, so it stays included: x ≤ {-k} uses a square bracket.

solution: Divide by {-a}, a negative number, so the sign turns round: x ≤ {-k}.

questions.prompt: Write {intervalIneq(a, b, ca, cb)} in interval notation.

misconceptions.explain: A square bracket means 'included' (≤); a round bracket means 'left out' (<).
Only an end with ≤ gets a square bracket.
An end with ≤ is included, so it gets a square bracket.

solution: {ca ? '≤ means the end ' + fmt(a) + ' is included: [' : '< means the end ' + fmt(a) + ' is left out: ('}.
{cb ? '≤ means ' + fmt(b) + ' is included: ]' : '< means ' + fmt(b) + ' is left out: )'}.

questions.prompt: Solve {poly([a, 'x'], [b, ''])} < {poly([c, 'x'], [d, ''])}. What is the largest whole number x can be?

misconceptions.explain: x < {(d - b) / (a - c)} leaves out {(d - b) / (a - c)} itself: the sign is <, not ≤.
Divide by {a - c} as well: {mono(a - c, 'x')} < {d - b} gives x < {(d - b) / (a - c)}.

solution: Collect x on the left: {mono(a - c, 'x')} < {d - b}.
Divide by {a - c}: x < {(d - b) / (a - c)}.
x must be less than {(d - b) / (a - c)}, so the largest whole number is {answer}.

misconceptions.explain: Dividing by the negative number {-a} turns ≥ into ≤.
The sign ≥ includes the end, so it stays included: x ≤ {-k} uses a square bracket.

solution: Divide by {-a}, a negative number, so the sign turns round: x ≤ {-k}.

questions.prompt: How many whole numbers x satisfy {lo} < {poly([2, 'x'], [q, ''])} ≤ {hi}?

misconceptions.explain: The left sign is <, so {(lo - q) / 2} itself is left out.
Divide every part by {2} before counting.

solution: Subtract {q} from all three parts: {lo - q} < {mono(2, 'x')} ≤ {hi - q}.
The whole numbers are {listStr(intsIn((lo - q) / 2, (hi - q) / 2, false, true))}: there are {answer}.
